extracted.intended_audience: Employers, industry stakeholders, regulatory commenters, and economists analyzing OSHA's proposed heat standard
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts employer duties and the agency's assumptions for requirements that must be met when the proposed initial heat trigger is met or exceeded, plus the methods OSHA used to estimate compliance costs and offsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drinking Water
rubrics_metrics.description: All affected establishments would be required to provide sufficiently cool water to their affected employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes establishments would purchase one 40‑quart cooler for every 40 employees and would purchase reusable water bottles for each affected employee (unit assumptions used to estimate costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coolers with Spigot (cost item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision/purchase of coolers with spigot to supply sufficiently cool water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's cost tables list one‑time annualized and annual costs by industry and region for 'Coolers with Spigot.' Agency assumption: one 40‑quart cooler per 40 employees. Used in the economic cost calculation (Table VIII.C.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reusable Water Bottle (cost item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision/purchase of reusable water bottles for each affected employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA includes tables of estimated one‑time annualized and annual costs by industry and region for 'Reusable Water Bottle.' These unit costs are used in total compliance cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Area(s) at Outdoor Work Sites
rubrics_metrics.description: All affected establishments would have to provide break areas for affected employees at outdoor work sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes each establishment with outdoor work sites would purchase a twelve‑by‑twelve‑foot tent as a means of providing artificial shade, and assumes this cost is incurred one time. This is captured in the agency's cost estimation for outdoor break area engineering controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outdoor Break Area Engineering Control (cost item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineering controls to provide outdoor break areas (e.g., shade structures) to protect affected employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA presents industry/region cost totals for 'Outdoor Break Area Engineering Control' in Table VIII.C.24. The text ties the assumed 12x12 tent purchase to these cost entries and reports subtotal and total costs by region/industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Area(s) and Work Area(s) at Indoor Work Sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishments with indoor work sites must provide break areas and work areas with sufficient air movement and humidity control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes establishments with indoor work sites would purchase one industrial pedestal fan and one dehumidifier that provide sufficient air movement and humidity control in break areas for every 10 employees, and the same control measures for work areas for every 10 employees. Note: OSHA does not capture a cost for dehumidifiers for establishments with indoor work sites in the four least humid States (Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, and Utah). These unit assumptions feed into the 'Air Movement' and 'Humidity Control' cost tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air Movement (cost item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision/purchase of air movement equipment (e.g., industrial pedestal fans) to provide sufficient air movement in indoor break/work areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA supplies detailed industry/region annualized and annual cost estimates for 'Air Movement.' The agency's unit assumption is one industrial pedestal fan per 10 employees for indoor break and work areas; these assumptions are used to generate the large tabulated cost totals (Table VIII.C.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humidity Control (cost item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision/purchase of dehumidifiers or other humidity control measures to control humidity in indoor break/work areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA provides industry/region cost totals for 'Humidity Control.' Important caveat: OSHA does not capture dehumidifier costs for indoor establishments in Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, and Utah (the four least humid States). Unit assumptions (one dehumidifier per 10 employees) and this geographic exception are explicitly used in cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization (new and returning employees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both new and returning employees would undergo acclimatization during their first week of work when the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded during that first week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA calculates acclimatization costs by multiplying unit costs (from Section VIII.C.IV.D.IV.) by the number of new employees and the number of returning employees. New employees are estimated using BLS JOLTS hire rates (June–Aug 2023) by sector to represent the percentage of employees that are new when the initial heat trigger is met; OSHA acknowledges limitations of using June–Aug hires and invites comment and better data. Returning employees are estimated by assuming two percent of all employees not newly hired qualify as returning (i.e., returning from an absence >14 days). OSHA multiplies the 2% by one minus the annual hire rate (from JOLTS) and then by the ratio of the summer hire rate to the annual hire rate to arrive at the percentage of returning employees present when the trigger is met. OSHA requests comment on these estimates and data sources that might improve them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest Breaks if Needed (if‑needed rest breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide if‑needed rest breaks when the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded (but not the high heat trigger); OSHA estimates the number and cost of such breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA calculates the expected number of rest breaks annually by using the number of work hours in a State for each shift type that meet or exceed the initial heat trigger but not the high heat trigger, normalizing hours to 8‑hour shift equivalents (divide hours by 8), and multiplying 8‑hour equivalents by the number of affected employees and the unit costs for rest breaks for indoor and outdoor employees (Section VIII.C.IV.D.V.). OSHA estimates that reductions in time spent pacing (increased worker efficiency) will partially offset the added cost of if‑needed rest breaks by 20% for outdoor employees and 23.33% for indoor employees; combining offsets and baseline noncompliance/exposure data, OSHA estimates ~21.78% of total cost of compliance with if‑needed rest breaks could be offset (~$0.0875B of $0.402B). The agency refers readers to Appendix A for more detail and notes the offset is applied in cost calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Communication (when initial trigger met)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers would be required to effectively communicate with affected employees when the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimates the number of times a designated person would have to perform this duty by estimating the number of hours annually that meet/exceed the initial heat trigger per State, normalizing to 8‑hour work shift equivalents, then multiplying these equivalents by the number of affected employees and unit costs. Unit cost assumption used: 15 seconds every two hours of both a designated person's and an at‑risk employee's time (see Section VIII.C.IV.D.VI.). These per‑time unit assumptions are used to calculate the total annualized costs listed in the tables.
